reasons: [alternatives_counterarguments/major] D1 [CL5; criteriaAssessments C5; alternatives (no 'reduce n4.large count now' option); practicalImplications] The draft says that, until requests are lowered, nodes cannot safely be removed and autoscaling 'will remove few nodes'. From that it concludes that right-sizing must come first (CL5, C5 assessment, 'Right-size ... then remove' alternative). The draft's own numbers contradict this. CPU requests are 72% of allocatable, about 115 of 160 vCPU. Memory requests are 68%, about 435 of 640 GiB. CL9 already finds that single-node loss fits inside the 28% request headroom. So the cluster can drop some nodes now, before any right-sizing. At an illustrative 85% request ceiling, CPU needs about 34 nodes and memory about 32. That means about 6 n4.large nodes could go, roughly 6 x 140.16 = ~840 USD/month at list price, subject to N+1, zone and PDB checks. The decision objective names 'cutting node count' as a separate alternative. The draft never assesses a direct node reduction on the current shape, and it gives no cluster-specific estimate, even an illustrative one, for any alternative. It leans instead on a generic vendor figure of 30-50% (E12). The decision-maker is left without the one quantified, low-risk option that could be acted on this month.
D1 major alternatives_counterarguments (direct node reduction omitted), remedy reanalysis

[reasoning_validity/major] D1 [verdict; CL15; CL12; criteriaAssessments C5; alternatives 'Reduce n4.large count now'; tradeoffs[1]; practicalImplications[1]; K16, K18, K21, K24] The new immediate node-cut estimate (CL15, C5 step 1, the 'Reduce n4.large count now' alternative, the verdict and practicalImplications) is inconsistent with its own safety condition. The draft sets an illustrative 85% request ceiling and sizes the fleet to the steady state: 40 x 72 / 85 = 33.88, so 34 nodes. It then shows (K21) that losing one node at 34 takes CPU requests to 87.3%, which breaches the ceiling the draft itself chose. It still presents 6 nodes / 840.96 USD/month as 'provided N+1 ... checks pass'. On the draft's own numbers, N+1 at 34 nodes fails an 85% ceiling. If the ceiling has to hold after losing one node, the fleet must satisfy (n-1) >= 33.88, so n = 35 and 5 nodes can go (700.80 USD/month). At 80%, (n-1) >= 36, so n = 37 and 3 nodes can go (420.48 USD/month). The N+1-consistent range is therefore 3-5 nodes, about 420-701 USD/month (7.5-12.5%), not 4-6 nodes and 561-841 USD/month (10-15%). The same flaw affects CL12's memory-bound floor: 32 nodes is exactly 85% memory requested at steady state, and N+1 at 31 nodes gives about 87.7%. The prior review (review-1 D1) proposed the ~6 nodes / ~840 USD figure without applying N+1, so the draft inherited the error by following it. The figure the review proposed was itself optimistic. Even so, the draft added and computed K21 and should have reconciled it. This is a production cluster, so the headline figure in the verdict overstates the safe immediate saving by about one node.
D1 major reasoning_validity (N+1 inconsistency), reanalysis; D3 minor needs internal request-peak data that web research cannot supply
